scene_title_sub: Ren meets his new client — and her PM
scene_desc: Ren arrives at Kurosawa Digital's office for the kickoff meeting. Saki greets him with a formal handshake and a thick requirements binder. Their styles clash immediately.
narrative_subplot: Ren is nervous but covers it with humor. Saki is unimpressed by his lack of documentation. First spark of tension.
notes: Phase 1 opener — establish characters and setting

scene_desc: Pulse Works receives Kurosawa Digital's official project charter for the XR platform build. The document reveals scope, objectives, and constraints.
key_terms_new: project,phase,deliverable,milestone,kickoff
key_term_defs: A temporary endeavor to create a unique product or result|A distinct stage in the project lifecycle with defined objectives|A tangible or intangible output produced during the project|A significant point or event in the project timeline|The initial meeting to formally start a project
narrative_subplot: Hina excitedly reads the charter aloud. Ren skims it — a habit Saki would disapprove of.
notes: Introduce Hina and first reference material

scene_desc: Director Kudo drops by the kickoff wrap-up with 'a few more ideas' that threaten to double the project scope. Ren scrambles; Saki takes notes calmly.
key_terms_new: stakeholder,sponsor,project manager
key_term_defs: An individual or group that may affect or be affected by the project|The person or group providing resources and support for the project|The person responsible for leading the project team and achieving objectives
review_concepts: Stakeholder identification & analysis
narrative_subplot: Director Kudo's casual scope additions frustrate Ren. Saki handles him diplomatically — Ren notices.
notes: Introduce Director Kudo as the wildcard stakeholder

scene_title_sub: Defining what's in and what's out
scene_desc: Ren and Saki face off over a whiteboard, arguing about what belongs in the MVP scope. Tetsu joins remotely, asking pointed questions about technical feasibility.
notes: Ren wants to keep scope loose for creativity. Saki insists on formal boundaries. Their argument is heated but productive.
column19: Introduce Tetsu — his first appearance via video call

scene_desc: Hina attempts to create a stakeholder register based on notes from the kickoff. She discovers the org chart is more complicated than expected.
key_terms_new: stakeholder register,power/interest grid,engagement level,influence,requirements
key_term_defs: A document listing all identified stakeholders and their attributes|A tool classifying stakeholders by their authority and concern|The degree to which a stakeholder is involved in the project|The ability of a stakeholder to affect project decisions|Conditions or capabilities needed by a stakeholder
reference_topic: Director Kudo's follow-up email with new 'suggestions'
narrative_subplot: Hina asks Ren why Saki was so formal at the meeting. Ren changes the subject.
notes: Deepen stakeholder analysis through practical artifact

scene_desc: Ren presents a draft scope statement to Saki. She redlines half of it. They negotiate line by line while Director Kudo's assistant sends yet another feature request.
key_terms_new: scope statement,WBS,work package,scope baseline
key_term_defs: A detailed description of the project scope including deliverables and boundaries|Work Breakdown Structure — a hierarchical decomposition of total project work|The lowest level of the WBS representing a manageable unit of work|The approved version of the scope statement and WBS
review_concepts: Project charter & business case;Stakeholder identification & analysis
narrative_subplot: Saki stays late to help Ren restructure the scope. She says it's 'just process.' Ren isn't sure.
notes: First collaborative moment between Ren and Saki

scene_desc: Ren and Hina interview Kurosawa Digital's end users about what they need from the XR platform. The answers are contradictory and overwhelming.
notes: Saki sends Ren a requirements template 'for reference' — her way of helping without admitting it.
column19: Show the messiness of real requirements gathering

scene_desc: Tetsu maps out the technical dependencies while Ren tries to build a realistic timeline. The gap between ambition and reality becomes clear.
key_terms_new: schedule,activity,dependency,lead time,lag time
key_term_defs: A model showing planned dates for project activities and milestones|A distinct unit of work performed during the project|A logical relationship between two activities|The amount of time a successor activity can be advanced|The amount of time a successor activity is delayed
narrative_subplot: Tetsu quietly notes he's already handling three other projects. Ren doesn't register the warning sign.
notes: Begin surfacing Tetsu's workload — foreshadowing bottleneck

scene_desc: During a planning session, Saki introduces the concept of critical path to Ren. He realizes several of Tetsu's tasks are on it — and Tetsu is already stretched thin.
key_terms_new: critical path,float,network diagram,forward pass
key_term_defs: The longest sequence of dependent activities determining the shortest project duration|The amount of time an activity can be delayed without delaying the project|A graphical representation of activity dependencies|A technique to calculate early start and early finish dates
review_concepts: Requirements gathering;Scope definition & WBS
narrative_subplot: Saki explains critical path with unexpected patience. Ren catches himself staring. Hina would notice if she were there.
notes: Ren's first moment of genuine respect for Saki's expertise

scene_title_sub: How long will this really take?
scene_desc: Pulse Works team debates estimates for the XR development sprints. Tetsu's conservative estimates clash with Ren's optimistic ones. Hina tries to mediate.
notes: Tetsu pushes back on aggressive timelines. Ren starts to see the systemic problem but doesn't name it yet.
column19: Set up the estimation vs. reality tension

scene_desc: Ren must present a cost estimate to Director Kudo. The numbers are higher than expected. Hina helps compile the data from vendor quotes and team rates.
key_terms_new: budget,cost estimate,contingency reserve,management reserve,cost baseline
key_term_defs: The approved spending plan for the project|An approximation of the monetary resources needed for project activities|Funds set aside to address identified risks|Funds reserved for unplanned changes to project scope and cost|The approved version of the time-phased project budget
narrative_subplot: Director Kudo pushes for a lower number. Ren feels the pressure of pleasing the client vs. being honest.
notes: First real budget pressure from the stakeholder

scene_title_sub: When the numbers don't add up
scene_desc: Saki reviews Ren's cost estimate and finds gaps. Their debate over contingency reserves reveals different risk philosophies. Director Kudo wants both PMs to 'make it work.'
key_terms_new: cost variance,earned value,planned value,actual cost
key_term_defs: The difference between earned value and actual cost|The value of work actually completed|The authorized budget assigned to scheduled work|The realized cost for work performed during a specific time period
review_concepts: Resource planning & estimation;Schedule management & critical path
narrative_subplot: Late-night email exchange about the budget. Saki signs off with 'Good night, Ren' instead of her usual formal closing. He reads it three times.
notes: Deepen the financial literacy and the subplot

scene_desc: A deployment stalls because three teams are waiting on Tetsu. Ren realizes the workflow is broken but doesn't know how to fix it. Saki mentions something called 'flow.'
notes: Saki lends Ren a book — The Phoenix Project. 'You might find it useful,' she says, avoiding eye contact.
column19: Introduce The Three Ways — the Phoenix Project bridge

scene_desc: Hina creates the team's first Kanban board on a whiteboard. It reveals how much work is piled on Tetsu compared to everyone else. The imbalance is shocking.
key_terms_new: flow,feedback loop,continuous learning,value stream,lead time (process)
key_term_defs: The movement of work through a system from start to finish|A mechanism for receiving information about output to improve process|The practice of ongoing experimentation and knowledge sharing|The sequence of activities required to deliver value to a customer|The total time from work request to work delivery
narrative_subplot: Hina draws the board and gasps at the imbalance. Tetsu just shrugs. Ren feels guilty.
notes: Visualize the bottleneck problem through a tangible artifact

scene_title_sub: Learning to limit work in progress
scene_desc: Ren tries implementing WIP limits after reading about them. The team resists. Tetsu quietly supports the experiment. The first week is painful but revealing.
key_terms_new: WIP limit,pull system,throughput,cycle time
key_term_defs: A constraint on the number of items allowed in a workflow stage at one time|A system where new work is started only when capacity is available|The amount of work completed in a given time period|The time it takes for a single item to move through the entire workflow
review_concepts: The Three Ways (flow; feedback; learning);Cost management & budgeting
narrative_subplot: Saki notices the Kanban board during a site visit. 'That's actually quite good,' she admits. Ren tries not to smile.
notes: First WIP limits experiment — learning from Phoenix Project

scene_title_sub: When production breaks on a Friday
scene_desc: The XR demo environment crashes before a client presentation. Tetsu is the only one who can fix it. Everyone waits. Ren sees the single-point-of-failure problem in real time.
narrative_subplot: Saki stays to help even though it's Company B's day off. She brings coffee. Ren notices she takes hers black.
notes: A crisis that exposes the bottleneck — and brings Ren and Saki closer

scene_desc: The team holds their first retrospective after the Friday crash. Hina takes detailed notes. The discussion reveals systemic issues nobody had acknowledged.
key_terms_new: retrospective,lessons learned,root cause,process improvement,action item
key_term_defs: A meeting held after a project phase or event to evaluate what went well and what didn't|Knowledge gained through project experience that can benefit future work|The fundamental reason for a problem or defect|A deliberate effort to enhance efficiency or effectiveness of a process|A documented task assigned to a team member with a deadline
narrative_subplot: Hina's notes accidentally include 'Saki brought Ren coffee — he smiled for the first time all day.' She crosses it out, but Ren sees it.
notes: Retrospective as both PM practice and subplot vehicle

scene_desc: Ren reviews the retrospective and realizes the crash followed a predictable pattern. He starts seeing connections between workload, dependencies, and failure.
key_terms_new: pattern recognition,process flow,bottleneck indicator,systemic risk
key_term_defs: The ability to identify recurring themes or issues in project data|The sequence of steps work follows through a system|A sign that a resource or process is constraining throughput|A risk arising from the way the system is structured rather than individual events
review_concepts: WIP limits;Requirements gathering
narrative_subplot: Ren texts Saki about the patterns he's seeing. Their conversation goes from work to 'what book are you reading?' He doesn't notice the time until 1am.
notes: Review earlier concepts while building analytical skills

scene_title_sub: Presenting the plan to the client
scene_desc: Ren and Saki jointly present the project roadmap to Director Kudo and the Kurosawa leadership team. It's their first time presenting together. The chemistry is professional but visible.
notes: They rehearse the presentation together the night before. Saki corrects his slides; he makes her delivery less stiff. They work well together. Both pretend not to notice.
column19: Major milestone — first joint presentation

scene_desc: Hina compiles a PM glossary for herself after feeling lost in meetings. Ren reviews it and realizes he's been learning these terms without noticing.
key_terms_new: baseline,variance,performance measurement,control account,work authorization
key_term_defs: An approved reference point used for comparison against actual results|The difference between planned and actual performance|The process of tracking and evaluating project progress|A management control point for scope, schedule, and cost integration|A formal approval to begin work on a specific project activity
narrative_subplot: Hina asks if Saki is 'always that intense.' Ren says yes, then adds, 'but she's really good at her job.' Hina raises an eyebrow.
notes: Vocabulary building through natural narrative context

scene_desc: Saki conducts a formal progress review against the baseline. The numbers show the project is slightly behind schedule but under budget. The team debates what this means.
key_terms_new: progress review,schedule variance,on track,behind schedule
key_term_defs: A formal evaluation of project progress against the planned baseline|The difference between the planned schedule and actual schedule progress|When actual progress matches or exceeds the planned baseline|When actual progress falls short of the planned baseline
review_concepts: Project lifecycle & phases;Scope definition & WBS
narrative_subplot: During the review, Saki and Ren's hands brush reaching for the same printout. Neither acknowledges it. Hina stifles a grin.
notes: Review earlier concepts through a formal checkpoint

scene_desc: Ren discovers a backlog of undocumented requests that team members have been handling informally. The hidden work is eating capacity and nobody tracked it.
notes: Tetsu finally admits he's been handling side requests from three Kurosawa departments. Ren is alarmed.
column19: Surface the hidden work problem from Phoenix Project

scene_desc: After discovering the hidden backlog, Ren categorizes all ongoing work using a framework Saki recommended. The results are eye-opening.
key_terms_new: business projects,internal projects,operational changes,unplanned work
key_term_defs: Work that directly delivers business value to external customers|Work that improves internal capabilities and infrastructure|Routine updates and maintenance activities|Firefighting and recovery work that disrupts planned activities
narrative_subplot: Saki recommended the framework via text with a bookmark emoji. Ren saved the message.
notes: Introduce The Four Types of Work from Phoenix Project

scene_title_sub: Bringing hidden work into the system
scene_desc: Ren restructures the Kanban board to include all four types of work. The team sees for the first time how much unplanned work they've been absorbing.
key_terms_new: unplanned work ratio,demand management,capacity allocation,visible workflow
key_term_defs: The proportion of unplanned work relative to total work — higher ratios indicate systemic instability|The practice of managing and prioritizing incoming work requests|Distributing available resources across different types of work|A system where all work items are tracked and visible to the team
review_concepts: The Three Ways (flow; feedback; learning);Stakeholder identification & analysis
narrative_subplot: Ren sends Saki a photo of the new board with the caption 'You were right.' She replies with a single thumbs-up. He wishes it were more.
notes: Review and synthesis of flow concepts

scene_title_sub: When the client sees the prototype
scene_desc: First prototype demo for Kurosawa Digital. The client's reaction is mixed — the tech is impressive but doesn't match their mental image. Expectations management becomes the topic.
notes: Director Kudo is publicly enthusiastic but privately tells Saki to 'fix it.' She doesn't tell Ren about the pressure.
column19: Prototype demo reveals expectation gaps

scene_title_sub: How PMs communicate up and down
scene_desc: Saki shares her communications management approach with Ren after the rocky demo. He realizes he's been informing but not managing expectations.
key_terms_new: communications management plan,stakeholder notification,information distribution,status meeting,escalation path
key_term_defs: A document defining who needs what information, when, and how|A targeted message to stakeholders about project events or decisions|The process of making relevant information available to stakeholders|A regular meeting to review project progress and address issues|A predefined process for raising issues to higher authority when needed
narrative_subplot: Saki teaches Ren her email template. He notices she has a structured approach to everything — even lunch orders. He finds it endearing.
notes: Bridge PMBOK communications with practical stakeholder management

scene_desc: Ren prepares for a one-on-one with Director Kudo to address the demo feedback. Saki coaches him on executive communication. The meeting goes better than expected.
key_terms_new: executive summary,RAG status,key message,audience analysis
key_term_defs: A brief overview of project status and decisions needed for senior stakeholders|Red-Amber-Green indicator showing project health at a glance|The core point a PM wants stakeholders to remember from a communication|The practice of tailoring communication style and content to the recipient
review_concepts: Resource planning & estimation;The Four Types of Work
narrative_subplot: Saki role-plays as Director Kudo so Ren can practice. She's terrifyingly accurate. They both laugh afterward — a first.
notes: Communications management through practical coaching

scene_desc: A critical module needs updating but Tetsu wrote it alone six months ago. Nobody else understands the code. The team confronts the knowledge silo problem.
notes: Tetsu opens up about feeling trapped — he can't take a day off without something breaking. Ren promises to fix the systemic issue, not just the symptom.
column19: Knowledge silos as a bottleneck — Phoenix Project theme

scene_desc: Ren initiates a knowledge-sharing program. Tetsu begins documenting his systems. Hina volunteers to be the first cross-trained team member.
key_terms_new: knowledge transfer,cross-training,bus factor,documentation,redundancy
key_term_defs: The process of sharing critical knowledge between team members|Training team members in skills outside their primary role|The number of people who would need to leave before a project stalls|Written records of systems, processes, and decisions for future reference|Having multiple people capable of performing critical tasks
reference_topic: Knowledge Gap Assessment — Pulse Works Team
narrative_subplot: Tetsu tells Ren this is the first time a PM actually tried to fix his workload instead of just adding to it.
notes: Address the bottleneck through systemic solutions

scene_desc: End of Phase 1. The team holds a major retrospective covering the first three months. The project is behind schedule but the team is stronger. Saki attends as a guest.
key_terms_new: phase gate,go/no-go decision,lessons learned register,phase review
key_term_defs: A formal checkpoint at the end of a project phase to evaluate progress|A decision point determining whether a project should continue to the next phase|A comprehensive document collecting insights from project experiences|A formal evaluation of a completed phase against its success criteria
review_concepts: WIP limits;Communications management;Project charter & business case
narrative_subplot: At the retrospective dinner, Saki sits next to Ren. Their conversation shifts from work to personal — favorite places, weekend routines. Hina takes a stealth photo of them talking.
notes: Phase 1 capstone — review and transition

scene_desc: Month 4. Tetsu calls in sick for the first time ever. Three workstreams grind to a halt. Ren finally sees the Theory of Constraints in action — the hard way.
notes: Saki helps Ren triage the crisis without being asked. She simply shows up. He's grateful but doesn't know how to say it.
column19: Phase 2 opener — the bottleneck becomes undeniable

scene_desc: Ren studies the workflow data to identify exactly where and why work gets stuck. The analysis confirms what everyone felt but nobody measured.
key_terms_new: constraint,throughput (system),exploitation,elevation,subordination
key_term_defs: Any factor that limits a system's ability to achieve its goal|The rate at which a system generates value or completes work|Making the most of the constraint's existing capacity without additional investment|Increasing the constraint's capacity through additional resources|Aligning all non-constraint resources to support the constraint
reference_topic: Updated Kanban Board — Bottleneck Analysis View
narrative_subplot: Hina creates a visualization that makes the bottleneck obvious. Ren realizes she's becoming genuinely skilled.
notes: Theory of Constraints terminology from Phoenix Project

scene_desc: Ren implements changes to protect Tetsu's capacity: routing requests through a queue, cross-training juniors, and blocking meeting interruptions.
key_terms_new: buffer,drum-buffer-rope,protective capacity,queue management
key_term_defs: Extra time or resources placed before a constraint to prevent starvation|A scheduling methodology derived from Theory of Constraints|Spare capacity in non-constraint resources to absorb variability|The practice of controlling the order and flow of work waiting to be processed
review_concepts: Theory of Constraints & bottleneck management;Cost management & budgeting
narrative_subplot: Saki quietly reassigns some of her own team's requests away from Tetsu. She doesn't mention it. Ren finds out from Hina.
notes: Apply ToC principles practically

scene_desc: Director Kudo casually requests a major feature addition during a status meeting. 'It shouldn't be that hard, right?' Ren and Saki must decide how to respond.
notes: Ren wants to push back directly. Saki suggests a more strategic approach. They strategize together over coffee — their first time meeting outside the office.
column19: Introduce change control through a classic scope creep scenario

scene_desc: Saki walks Ren through Kurosawa Digital's formal change control process. It's bureaucratic but Ren starts to see why it exists.
key_terms_new: change request,change control board (CCB),impact analysis,change log,configuration management
key_term_defs: A formal proposal to modify any project baseline or document|A group responsible for reviewing and approving or rejecting change requests|An assessment of the effect a proposed change would have on scope schedule and cost|A comprehensive record of all changes requested and their disposition|A system for maintaining consistency of a product's attributes with its design
reference_topic: CR-0042 — Add AR Filter Feature to XR Platform
narrative_subplot: Saki explains change control with genuine passion. Ren teases her about being excited by paperwork. She almost smiles.
notes: Formalize change management vocabulary

scene_title_sub: Using impact analysis to manage expectations
scene_desc: Ren presents an impact analysis of Director Kudo's feature request. The numbers make the case clearly: adding the feature would delay launch by six weeks.
key_terms_new: scope creep,gold plating,impact assessment,trade-off analysis
key_term_defs: Uncontrolled expansion of project scope without corresponding adjustments to time cost and resources|Adding features or improvements beyond what is required by the project scope|A systematic evaluation of the consequences of a proposed change|Comparing the benefits and drawbacks of different options to make an informed decision
review_concepts: Change control & integrated change management;Schedule management & critical path
narrative_subplot: Director Kudo accepts the data grudgingly. Afterward, Saki texts Ren: 'Well played.' He saves the message.
notes: Review change control and scheduling through a real decision

scene_desc: After the scope creep scare, Ren realizes the project has no formal risk management. Saki helps him set up the first risk identification workshop.
notes: During the workshop, Ren and Saki finish each other's sentences. Tetsu and Hina exchange a look.
column19: Introduce risk management — a PMBOK core knowledge area

scene_desc: The team builds their first risk register. Each risk gets a probability, impact, and response strategy. Some risks are technical; others are political.
key_terms_new: risk,risk register,probability,impact,risk response strategy
key_term_defs: An uncertain event or condition that if it occurs has a positive or negative effect on project objectives|A document recording identified risks their assessment and planned responses|The likelihood that a risk event will occur|The effect on project objectives if the risk event occurs|A planned approach to address a risk — avoid mitigate transfer or accept
narrative_subplot: Hina adds 'Ren and Saki's arguments' as a risk. Ren makes her delete it. She grins.
notes: Build risk management vocabulary through artifact creation

scene_desc: A vendor delay that was on the risk register actually happens. The team activates their response plan — and it mostly works. The 'mostly' part teaches valuable lessons.
key_terms_new: risk trigger,issue,contingency plan,risk owner,workaround
key_term_defs: A predefined event or condition that indicates a risk is about to occur or has occurred|A risk that has materialized and requires immediate action|A predefined response plan activated when a specific risk occurs|The person responsible for monitoring and managing a specific risk|An unplanned response to a negative risk event that was not previously identified
review_concepts: Risk identification & response planning;Theory of Constraints & bottleneck management
narrative_subplot: Ren and Saki manage the crisis together seamlessly. Tetsu observes: 'You two have gotten good at this.' Awkward silence.
notes: Review risk and ToC through a real incident

scene_desc: User testing reveals quality issues in the XR prototype. Ren wants to ship anyway; Saki insists on standards. Their debate exposes different quality philosophies.
notes: Ren sees that Saki's insistence on quality comes from caring about the end users, not just process. His perspective on her shifts.
column19: Introduce quality management through a genuine tension

scene_desc: The team establishes quality metrics for the XR platform. Hina creates a quality dashboard. The numbers tell a different story than gut feelings.
key_terms_new: quality management plan,quality metric,quality assurance,quality control,acceptance criteria
key_term_defs: A document describing how quality policies and standards will be implemented|A measurable indicator used to assess whether quality requirements are being met|Proactive processes to prevent defects and ensure standards|Reactive inspection of deliverables to identify defects|Predefined conditions that must be met for deliverables to be accepted
narrative_subplot: Hina creates a quality checklist and adds 'Would Saki approve?' as the final item. Ren pretends to be annoyed.
notes: Quality management vocabulary and measurement

scene_desc: Saki's quality review rejects a key deliverable. The team must rework it. The experience teaches the difference between quality assurance and quality control.
key_terms_new: rework,defect,cost of quality,prevention cost,appraisal cost
key_term_defs: Effort required to correct defective or nonconforming deliverables|An imperfection or deficiency that reduces the quality of a deliverable|The total cost of ensuring quality including prevention appraisal and failure costs|Investment in processes and tools to prevent defects from occurring|Cost of evaluating deliverables to ensure they meet quality standards
review_concepts: Quality management;Change control & integrated change management
narrative_subplot: Saki apologizes for the harsh review. Ren says she was right. It's the first time he's said that without it being an argument. Something shifts.
notes: Review quality and change management

scene_title_sub: When teams talk past each other
scene_desc: A miscommunication between Pulse Works developers and Kurosawa Digital's design team causes a two-week rework. The root cause is unclear requirements handoff.
notes: Ren and Saki realize they've been communicating well with each other but not cascading that clarity to their teams. They start syncing daily.
column19: Communications breakdown as a real PM challenge

scene_title_sub: Is there a better way to work?
scene_desc: After repeated handoff problems, Ren researches agile methodologies. The team debates whether to pivot their approach mid-project.
key_terms_new: agile,sprint,iteration,user story,product backlog
key_term_defs: An iterative and incremental approach to project management emphasizing flexibility and customer feedback|A time-boxed iteration typically 1-4 weeks during which a set of work is completed|A single cycle of development within an iterative approach|A short description of a feature from the end user's perspective|A prioritized list of features and requirements for the product
narrative_subplot: Hina asks if agile means they can 'move faster.' Tetsu says it means they can 'fail faster and learn.' Ren realizes that's The Second Way.
notes: Introduce agile — a key PMBOK methodology

scene_desc: Ren proposes a hybrid approach: keeping PMBOK governance for stakeholder reporting while using agile sprints for development. Saki is skeptical but willing to try.
key_terms_new: hybrid approach,sprint planning,daily standup,sprint review,sprint retrospective
key_term_defs: Combining elements of predictive and agile methodologies based on project needs|A collaborative meeting to define the sprint goal and select backlog items|A brief daily meeting for the team to synchronize activities and identify blockers|A meeting at sprint end to demonstrate completed work and gather feedback|A meeting for the team to reflect on the sprint process and identify improvements
review_concepts: Communications management;Risk identification & response planning
narrative_subplot: Saki agrees to the hybrid approach on one condition: they review it together weekly. Ren agrees a little too quickly.
notes: Hybrid methodology as a practical compromise

scene_desc: The team evolves their simple Kanban board into a proper workflow management system. WIP limits are enforced digitally. The improvement in flow is measurable.
notes: Tetsu admits the Kanban system has genuinely reduced his stress. He offers to buy Ren lunch — high praise from Tetsu.
column19: Formalize Kanban as a management tool

scene_desc: Hina documents the team's Kanban practices. The board has evolved from a simple task tracker to a communication tool that makes work status instantly visible.
key_terms_new: Kanban board,swim lane,WIP indicator,blocked item,cumulative flow diagram
key_term_defs: A visual tool displaying work items in columns representing workflow stages|A horizontal row on a Kanban board separating work by category or team|A visual signal showing current WIP count against the WIP limit|A work item that cannot progress due to an impediment|A chart showing the count of items in each workflow stage over time
reference_topic: Pulse Works Kanban Board v3.0 — Mature State
narrative_subplot: Hina's documentation is thorough and clear. Ren realizes she doesn't need his guidance as much anymore. He's proud and a little sad.
notes: Kanban vocabulary and visual management maturity

scene_desc: The team experiences their first 'flow' week — no major blockers, WIP limits holding, predictable throughput. It feels almost too good. Ren waits for something to break.
key_terms_new: flow efficiency,service level expectation,steady state,continuous delivery
key_term_defs: The ratio of active work time to total lead time for a work item|A target for how quickly work items should move through the system|A condition where workflow rates are predictable and sustainable|The practice of keeping work in a releasable state at all times
review_concepts: Kanban & visual management;WIP limits;The Four Types of Work
narrative_subplot: Saki visits the Pulse Works office to see the Kanban board in person. She stays longer than necessary. Ren walks her to the station. Neither mentions it the next day.
notes: Review flow concepts through achievement

scene_title_sub: Is the project really on track?
scene_desc: Mid-project. Director Kudo asks if they're on budget. Ren says 'probably.' Saki says 'let's find out for real.' She introduces earned value management — and the numbers are sobering.
notes: Saki teaches Ren EVM over dinner — work dinner, she clarifies. Ren doesn't correct her when the conversation drifts to weekend plans.
column19: Introduce EVM as a powerful but initially intimidating tool

scene_desc: Ren and Hina work through the EVM calculations. The metrics reveal the project is over budget and behind schedule — but not by as much as feared.
key_terms_new: EVM,CPI,SPI,EAC,TCPI
key_term_defs: Earned Value Management — a method for measuring project performance against the plan|Cost Performance Index — ratio of earned value to actual cost (CPI > 1 is good)|Schedule Performance Index — ratio of earned value to planned value (SPI > 1 is good)|Estimate at Completion — predicted total cost of the project based on current performance|To-Complete Performance Index — required future efficiency to meet budget target
narrative_subplot: Hina declares EVM 'actually kind of cool' once she understands it. She creates a color-coded dashboard. Saki is impressed.
notes: EVM vocabulary and calculation

scene_desc: Armed with EVM data, Ren presents a recovery plan to the steering committee. The data makes the conversation about facts, not feelings. Director Kudo respects the approach.
key_terms_new: variance at completion,schedule recovery,cost recovery,performance baseline,trend analysis
key_term_defs: The projected difference between the budget at completion and the estimate at completion|Actions taken to bring a behind-schedule project back on track|Actions taken to bring an over-budget project back within budget constraints|The integrated scope schedule and cost baselines used as a reference for performance measurement|Examining project performance data over time to identify patterns and predict future performance
review_concepts: Earned value management (EVM);Quality management;Agile & hybrid approaches
narrative_subplot: Director Kudo congratulates both PMs publicly. Under the table, Saki squeezes Ren's hand briefly. He freezes. She pretends nothing happened.
notes: Review EVM and earlier concepts through a decision point

scene_title_sub: When you can't build it yourself
scene_desc: A critical XR component needs to be outsourced. Ren has never managed a vendor relationship. Saki has — but Kurosawa Digital's procurement process is famously slow.
notes: Ren asks Saki about vendor management over lunch. It's definitely not a date. They both ordered the same thing. Hina is keeping score.
column19: Introduce procurement as a PMBOK knowledge area

scene_desc: Ren and Hina evaluate three vendors for the XR component. Each has strengths and risks. The decision matrix reveals that the cheapest option is also the riskiest.
key_terms_new: procurement management plan,make-or-buy analysis,vendor evaluation,request for proposal (RFP),contract type
